title: Big Four valuation teams use AI for peer screening, volatility and research
problem: Valuation engagements involve repetitive analytical and research steps that consume junior analyst hours.
approach: A KPMG panellist said the firm is embedding AI into everything it does, including peer screening, volatility and customer-attrition analysis.
Other Big Four panellists said AI is increasingly part of valuation workflows and stressed judgment, review and auditability; no tools named.
Panellists called reviewer sign-off on AI-assisted analyses essential; several said firms are hiring fewer entry-level analysts (self-reported, no figures).
who: KPMG and other Big Four panellists

title: Plain-language research agent over private-company deal and discount datasets
problem: Valuers search transaction and discount databases by hand, filtering and re-filtering comparables as they learn more about the subject company.
approach: BVR announced an agent that answers plain-language questions over its transaction, control-premium and marketability-discount datasets, returning calculations, tables and graphs.
A Display Transactions feature opens the underlying observations, and Saved Threads keeps research for later refinement.
BVR describes comparable analysis moving from hours to seconds (vendor-published, no measurement).
The analyst reviews the underlying transactions, decides which suit the subject company, and owns the conclusion.

title: Vendor valuation platform for multiples and discount-rate research (AI use not stated)
problem: Manual research for valuation multiples and discount rates is a significant time drain for smaller valuation teams.
approach: Kreston Reeves and Rouse use Valutico's comparable-data analysis and automated data integration; the case studies do not say generative AI was used.
Rouse is quoted as cutting project time by a third, saving up to a day at a time (vendor-published).
Kreston Reeves says research is quicker; the vendor's wording is at least 3-5 times faster (vendor-published, no firm-specific figure).
The analyst selects and justifies the multiples and discount-rate inputs.

title: Research assistant over a valuation technical library, used for coaching junior analysts
problem: Reviewers answer the same technical questions repeatedly, and juniors need to learn concepts such as owner-compensation normalization and company-specific risk premium.
approach: BVR announced an assistant that answers plain-language questions with summaries drawn from its vetted content, including case law, guides and webinars.
A BVWire tip suggests sending junior analysts to the assistant first, then reviewing how they applied the concept.
A senior reviews the junior's conclusions and how the concept was applied. No outcome figure is published.

title: AI assistant inside Excel for building, auditing and flexing valuation models
problem: Valuation models live in Excel, and building, auditing and flexing them is manual.
approach: Anthropic says Claude in Excel builds financial models from filings and data feeds, audits formulas across linked workbooks and runs sensitivity analyses.
A BVR and CBV workshop (April 2025) covered Copilot in Excel as a personal assistant for valuation practitioners.
Anthropic reports a FundamentalLabs Excel agent scored 83% on complex tasks and passed 5 of 7 Financial Modeling World Cup levels (vendor-published).
The analyst reviews model logic and outputs.

title: Idea: forecasting full statements beyond one year for discounted cash flow valuation
problem: Idea, not a deployment: in discounted cash flow valuation most value sits beyond the first forecast year, yet few tools forecast full statements over long horizons.
approach: Researchers released a benchmark and a specialist model forecasting 78 statement line items 1 to 20 quarters ahead; not a language-model agent.
On the benchmark it beat classical machine learning and frontier language models, more so at longer horizons (independent). No firm use found.
The valuer would set scenario assumptions and judge whether projections are reasonable.

title: Idea: language-model price estimates as a cross-check in property appraisal
problem: Idea, not a deployment: property price estimates normally rely on statistical models or comparable sales that need specialist set-up.
approach: Researchers tested leading language models on international housing datasets using zero-shot, few-shot, market-report and hybrid prompts. No firm deployment found.
Traditional machine learning stayed stronger on accuracy; language models gave meaningful estimates but were overconfident in price intervals (independent).
The appraiser evaluates the output's credibility and owns the conclusion.

title: Template-driven valuation report generation in a vendor platform (AI use not stated)
problem: Long business valuation reports, 200 pages in one case, can take months to assemble, and manual work leaves room for errors.
approach: RXM (Singapore) and PKF FI use Valutico's automated report generation; the case studies do not say generative AI was used.
RXM's director is quoted saying a 200-page valuation went from months to days, saving hundreds of hours (vendor-published).
PKF FI says it saved time and drastically reduced error risk, with no error counts; the vendor cites 3-5 times faster (vendor-published).
The valuer reviews the generated report before issue.

title: Generative AI drafts parts of valuation reports such as market commentary
problem: Report writing is time-consuming, and some narrative sections, such as market commentary, are routine.
approach: The IVSC paper (July 2025) says some valuers already use ChatGPT or other public AI for report writing, such as market commentary.
A BVR webinar (November 2025) says it demonstrates drafting report sections; no firm is named and no outcome figure is published.
The valuer keeps control of content and verifies data sources and facts.

title: AI reviewer agents check valuations against standards and review policy before sign-off
problem: Reports can have every required section yet contain inconsistent requirements, unsupported assumptions or arguments an opposing party could raise, and reviewers must check many positions on deadline.
approach: AICPA FVS podcast speakers described standards-analyzer and adversarial-reviewer agents; Anthropic's May 2026 release lists a Valuation reviewer template. No named deployment.
The Anthropic template checks valuations against comparables, methodology and the firm's review standards; the managed-agent version adds a full audit log.
The valuer reviews and decides on each flag, and the signing valuer remains responsible. No outcome figure is published.

title: Idea: anticipating AI-generated critiques of a valuation report
problem: Idea, not a deployment: clients and counterparties feed reports into AI and return detailed challenges to assumptions, methods and conclusions, sometimes before the analyst is retained.
approach: NACVA speakers advised valuers to anticipate machine review when writing, ask to see the client's prompt and output, and respond with evidence.
They also advised setting expectations about AI in the engagement letter. This is advice, not a documented deployment.
The valuer judges whether each AI-raised challenge has merit.

title: End-to-end valuation agent from financial documents to model, report and deck
problem: Production work, including data entry, model build, and report and deck assembly, takes most of the time in a valuation engagement.
approach: Startup Dealgauge says it turns financial documents into client-ready valuation reports, Excel models and decks so valuations finish in hours (vendor-published).
Valutico advertises auto-generated forecasts and defensible deal valuations in minutes, not weeks (vendor-published). No named customers.
The valuer reviews the model, assumptions and conclusion; IVSC says the valuer must keep full control.

title: Portfolio valuation platform extracts company data with AI to standardize fund valuations
problem: Fund valuations were built in bespoke spreadsheets from whatever public data was at hand; the process was manual and resource-intensive.
approach: Hamilton Lane says it partnered with 73 Strings to standardize valuations on one platform that uses AI to process valuation data.
Its director of valuation says the process is now systematized and efficient (self-reported, no time or accuracy figure).
A Eurazeo executive is quoted crediting the platform with significant ROI (vendor-published, no figure).
73 Strings says human judgement stays central; who reviews marks at Hamilton Lane is not described.

title: Valuation firms package portfolio valuation as AI-enabled platforms (Stout Drivr, Kroll REVS)
problem: Alternative asset managers run fragmented, manual valuation workflows with the valuation provider as a separate hand-off, and want more frequent, transparent valuations.
approach: Stout announced Drivr on 2026-07-14, with AI-powered data extraction and its independent valuation opinions inside the workflow.
Kroll announced REVS on 2026-03-03, an AI-enabled real estate platform with workflow automation and audit-ready documentation.
Stout's co-leader says teams can move in hours or days, not weeks (self-reported, no measurement).
Valuation practitioners issue Stout's opinions; Kroll's release does not describe human checkpoints.

title: CohnReznick builds a vendor's AI-enabled analytics into its fund valuation work
problem: General partners are asked for valuations that are more frequent, faster and more traceable amid investor scrutiny and compressed timelines, often without matching budget or headcount.
approach: CohnReznick announced (page dated 2026-03-26) that its Valuation Advisory practice is incorporating 73 Strings' AI-enabled analytics into its established methodologies.
It says this adds consistency across models and deeper insight into valuation drivers, and accelerates certain aspects of the process.
It says valuations will be faster, more transparent and more defensible (self-reported, no measurement).
Valuation professionals keep judgment on complex inputs, scenario analysis and conclusions.
